name: Drivacor
description: Drivacor is a dopaminergic motivation amplifier that targets the mesolimbic reward pathway and anterior cingulate cortex to generate intense, directed motivational drive toward goals the user holds at the time of dosing. Unlike stimulants, it does not increase energy or wakefulness broadly — it creates a laser-focused sense of purpose and urgency around specific tasks, making the user feel that their work is not just important but essential. It is the most used performance pharmaceutical in GLMZ's Tier 3-4 white-collar workforce.
effects: heightened sense of purpose and task urgency
subjective sense that current work is deeply meaningful
side_effects: motivation narrows to whatever goal was active at dosing — other priorities feel irrelevant and can be neglected dangerously
post-dose motivational crash — anhedonia and goal-apathy lasting 12–24 hours
chronic use associated with natural dopamine system degradation — baseline motivation drops, requiring escalating doses
users may pursue misaligned goals with Drivacor intensity — including harmful ones
relationship neglect is statistically the most common side effect in long-term users
cultural_context: Drivacor is GLMZ's productivity religion made chemical. Tier 3-4 culture openly celebrates it — people post their Drivacor-fueled work sprints on social feeds, joke about their 'push days,' and treat the motivational crash as a badge of dedication. Helix has successfully positioned Drivacor as self-improvement rather than dependency. The uglier reality is visible in Tier 3 burnout clinics, which are full of former Drivacor heavy users whose natural dopamine systems have been ground down to baseline dysfunction. On the Shelf, a cruder street version called 'fire pills' uses a different mechanism — more stimulant than motivator — and is used by gig workers who need to string together 20-hour shifts.
story_hooks: A Tier 3 architect built his career on Drivacor. He's just been diagnosed with severe dopamine system degradation — he can no longer feel motivated about anything without the drug, and the drug is making it worse. He has six months before the damage may be permanent.

A Shelf fixer took Drivacor before a job and found herself Drivacor-locked onto a secondary goal she'd been thinking about at dosing — finding her missing sister — instead of the job she was paid for. She completed the job anyway. She has no memory of how.
Helix's internal data shows Drivacor's dopamine degradation rates are four times higher than their public clinical trials indicated. Someone in their research division wants that data out.
